newsitem.title: USA: EU official--opportunity for deal in meat talks.
newsitem.headline: EU official--opportunity for deal in meat talks.

text.p: A senior European Union negotiator said Thursday that he sees an opportunity to reach an agreement with the United States over an escalating dispute on meat imports.
"There should be the opportunity to strike a deal," said Lars Hoelgaard, the senior EU negotiator at the ongoing bilateral talks on meat import inspection regulations.
In a briefing with the press after two-and-a-half days of talks with U.S. officials, Hoelgaard said he was "much more optimistic" about the outcome of the talks than he was a week ago.
The EU delegation had been scheduled to leave Washington later Thursday, but Hoelgaard announced at a press briefing that the European officials would be staying on for another day of talks.
He said he hoped that "by this time tomorrow" they would have an agreement in hand.
EU and U.S. officials have been meeting all week to reach an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks.

The talks ended last week without an agreement by an April 1 deadline. Both sides then imposed new regulations that threatened to stop up to $100 million worth of U.S. poultry and dairy products going to Europe and halt some $300 million worth of European meat products being shipped to the United States.
Hoelgaard said that negotiators had been able to resolve issues over dairy exports and that "there should be no problem" with the United States continuing to ship dairy products to the EU.
He said that the major difficulties left were in the poultry sector, specifically decontamination methods.
"The major stumbling block ... at this stage ... remains the issue of what kind of decontamination methods the EU would be able to accept for the poultry sector," Hoelgaard said.

Negotiators are trying to reach an agreement before April 15, when the United States has said it would remove over 100 European meat and poultry plants from its list of approved exporters if the plants do not comply with U.S. standards.
Hoelgaard said he hoped such action could be avoided.
"We do have an opportunity here to avoid ... a serious setback if such action were to be taken," he said.
